body_ar:
الوسوسة طاعة للشيطان.
السؤال: أجد وسوسة في الغسل فأمضي ثلاثين دقيقة أو خمساً وأربعين دقيقة وأنا في الغسل، فيضيع الكثير من الوقت وكلما غسلت عضواً يخيل إلي أنني لم أغسله، فأرجع إليه، وكذلك شعر الرأس أو اللحية، فيضيع فيه الكثير من الوقت؟
الجواب: هذا الإنسان مصاب بوسوسة، وهي من عمل الشيطان، فعليه أن يحذر أن يجعل للشيطان عليه سبيلاً، وعليه ألا يطيع الشيطان وهو يعلم أنه عدوه، بل عليه أن يطيع الله، وأن يجتنب عمل الشيطان، وإذا أخبره الشيطان بأنه لم يفعل، فليرغم أنف الشيطان وليترك ما ألقى عليه. ومن هنا، فالذي يشعر بالوسوسة عليه أن يكثر من التعوذ بالله من الشيطان الرجيم، صادقاً بقلبه، وعليه ألا يتبع وساوس الشيطان، فإذا غسل عضواً تجاوزه وغسل غيره، وإذا خيل إليه الشيطان أنه لم ينته فلا يراجع نفسه في ذلك، ولا ينظر إليه، لأنه قد يريه الشيطان أنه لم يغسل بعد...
body_en:
## Obsessive misgiving is obedience to Satan

**The question:** I find obsessive misgiving (waswasah) in the full ritual washing (ghusl), so that I spend thirty or forty-five minutes at it. A great deal of time is wasted, and every time I have washed a limb it seems to me that I have not washed it, so I go back to it — and the same with the hair of the head, or the beard — and a great deal of time is wasted in it.

**The answer:** This person is afflicted with obsessive misgiving, and it is of Satan's doing. He must beware of giving Satan a way against him. He must not obey Satan while knowing that he is his enemy; rather he must obey God, and keep away from Satan's doing. And when Satan tells him that he has not done a thing, let him rub Satan's nose in the dust and abandon what has been cast upon him.

Accordingly, whoever feels obsessive misgiving must take often to seeking refuge with God from the accursed Satan, truthful in his heart; and he must not follow Satan's promptings. So when he has washed a limb, let him pass on from it and wash another; and if Satan makes it seem to him that he has not finished, let him not go back over himself in that, nor look at it — because Satan may make him see that he has not yet washed …

options: render with an excerpt banner and link the .doc
flags.note: Excerpt only, style guide section 9. It breaks off on an ellipsis mid-sentence, in the middle of the practical instruction, with the first question answered in substance but the sitting unfinished. The complete text sits behind /medias/doc/d-a-96.doc. The English ends exactly where the Arabic ends and completes nothing. Must not be rendered as a whole lesson.

flags.context: the heading, the question and the answer throughout
flags.note: The term has two lives in the tradition and the English must not blur them. Literally 'وسوسة' is a whispering, and in the answer it is Satan's act — the Sheikh says so explicitly and the heading says so. But in the question it names the condition the questioner suffers from: an intrusive, repeating doubt about whether an act of purification has been performed, which the jurists treat as a recognised affliction with its own rules. 'Whispering' alone carries the first and loses the second; 'obsessive misgiving' carries the second and the Arabic in brackets recovers the first. The rendering is deliberately not a clinical term: the Sheikh is not diagnosing and the English must not appear to.

flags.arabic: فعليه أن يحذر ... وعليه ألا يطيع ... بل عليه أن يطيع الله
flags.context: the Sheikh's instructions in the answer
options: he must beware / he must not obey / he must obey
it is obligatory (wājib) upon him to beware
flags.note: A point where the fixed mapping must NOT be reached for. 'عليه أن' states a duty, and in this answer it is stated four times, but the Sheikh uses no term from the five-rulings table anywhere — not wājib, not makrūh, not ḥarām. Writing 'obligatory (wājib)' into the English would put a classification in his mouth that he did not give, which the style guide forbids. 'Must' carries the force of 'عليه أن' without importing a grading. Conversely 'should' would weaken it.

flags.context: the Sheikh's instruction in the answer
options: let him rub Satan's nose in the dust
flags.note: A fixed Arabic idiom, literally to press another's nose into the dust, meaning to humble and defeat him. The image is kept rather than paraphrased because it is doing rhetorical work in a passage of pastoral advice: the questioner is being told to act against the misgiving deliberately and with contempt for it.

flags.arabic: إذا غسل عضواً تجاوزه وغسل غيره
flags.context: the practical instruction at the end of the served answer
options: when he has washed a limb, let him pass on from it and wash another
if he washes a part of the body he should move past it and wash the next
flags.note: 'عضو' in the context of ghusl is a limb or bodily part as the jurists enumerate them. The instruction is the operative content of the fatwa — do not repeat, move on — and the text breaks off in the middle of the reasoning that supports it. A reader gets the instruction but not the whole of its ground.

translator_notes: One of three records, IDs 722-724, filed in the written-fatwa section and uploaded on 10 May 2011 within about half an hour of one another. Unlike most of that section, each of the three carries a real written question and a real written answer, and none is a title-only stub. All three are nonetheless excerpts: each breaks off after the first question and the full sitting sits behind a .doc or .docx download in the /medias/doc/d-a-* series.

The source's final line, 'تحميل المادة' ('download the material'), is the label of a download link in the page furniture, not part of the text. It is recorded as source_download_link and omitted from body_ar and body_en.

A genuine written fatwa with a complete question and a substantively complete answer, and the clearest case in this slice for why the under-200-character rule cannot be used to classify these records: it is short, and it is not a stub.

The record has no site synopsis and no opening formula; it begins directly with a heading that states the answer's conclusion before the question is put. The heading is the site's editorial framing, not the Sheikh's words, and should be marked as such where the site displays it.
The questioner's wording is kept in the first person as served, including the repeated complaint about wasted time, which is what the answer responds to.
No ruling term from the five-rulings table appears anywhere in the record. The duties stated in the answer are expressed with 'عليه أن' and no grading is given; see the flag.
